title: mmz fragment
description: Configuration for a file named in a manifest's imports: list. A fragment declares scopes, probes and commands, and may itself import; it may not set cache_dir, gitignore, strict or on_hit — those are root-manifest-only policy keys, and setting one in a fragment is a load error.

imports.description: Paths to other YAML files whose scopes, probes and commands are merged into this one. A directory entry expands to every *.yaml and *.yml file directly inside it (not recursive), sorted lexically; a missing file or directory is an error, an empty directory is not. Relative paths resolve against the directory of the file that names them, not the project root, so a fragment can reference a sibling fragment; absolute paths (store paths included) are used as written. A fragment may declare imports of its own. A key declared in two files is an error naming both; cache_dir, gitignore, strict and on_hit may only be set in the root manifest.

scopes.description: Named glob sets, each referenced by command rules. A scope is either an array of patterns, or an object naming those patterns under globs alongside a per-scope gitignore override.

oneOf.description: The scope's patterns; the manifest-level gitignore setting applies.
The scope's patterns plus an optional per-scope gitignore override.

globs.description: The scope's patterns. At least one is required; use the array form when there is no override to declare.

gitignore.description: Overrides the manifest-level gitignore for this scope only; omit to inherit it. Set false for a scope naming build artifacts: they live in git-ignored paths by definition, so under the filter the scope resolves empty and the rules referencing it are fresh forever.

probes.description: Named sources of input bytes. A rule's inputs references a probe by name exactly as it references a scope, and the hash of what the probe produced joins that rule's input digest — which is how a rule depends on part of a file (one node of a flake.lock, one recipe body out of a Justfile) or on something that is not a file at all (a toolchain fingerprint). A probe reads either a file (`file`, which needs a `json` or `ast` selector) or the stdout of a command (`run`); the two are mutually exclusive, and a probe must declare one. One namespace with scopes: a probe sharing a name with a scope is a manifest error. A probe is resolved once per mmz invocation, however many rules name it. Weigh the trade before reaching for one: a wrong scope costs time, a wrong probe can lie.

run.description: The command line whose stdout is the probe's bytes, run by `sh -c` from the project root with stdin closed. Mutually exclusive with `file`. A non-zero exit is a hard error naming the probe, its exit code, and its stderr: mmz exits without consuming the output and without writing a record, so a failed command never reaches the hasher. A probe that cannot be spawned is the same error. Content correctness and determinism are the manifest author's, not mmz's — pin the ordering, strip the timestamps, and assert the shape inside the probe (jq -e, a schema check) so a bad shape becomes a non-zero exit, or hand the shape to `json` below and let mmz enforce it.

file.description: A file to read, relative to the project root — the same base scope globs resolve against. Mutually exclusive with `run`, and requires a selector — `json` for a document, `ast` for source code. This is the fully in-process shape: no process is spawned, nothing has to be on PATH, and there is no shell quoting to get wrong, so a rule can depend on one field of a lockfile that a scope could only name whole. A file that is missing or unreadable is a hard error naming the probe and the path. Hashing a whole file is what a scope is for, which is why a bare `file` with no selector is refused rather than accepted as a second spelling of one.

json.description: A jq program selecting out of the probe's bytes, run in-process by an embedded jq engine — no jq on PATH. mmz hashes its own canonical rendering of the selected value, object keys sorted at every depth and array order preserved, so a renderer's key order is structurally not an input and nobody has to remember jq -S. Multiple outputs (`.a, .b`) join one per line. A selection that measured nothing — no output at all, or a lone null — is a hard error, for the same reason jq -e exists: a probe tracking null reports one digest whatever the document does, leaving the rule fresh forever against an input nobody is measuring. `false` is a value and passes. Bytes that are not exactly one JSON value, a program that does not compile, and a program that raises against the document are each a hard error naming the probe.

ast.description: An ast-grep pattern matching over the probe's bytes parsed as source code, run in-process by a bundled tree-sitter grammar — nothing on PATH, no regex pretending to be a parser. Mutually exclusive with `json`. mmz hashes its own canonical rendering of every matched node — every token exactly, the whitespace between them dropped — so reformatting a signature is not an edit to it, while renaming one is. A match is a whole node unless `capture` narrows it to the metavariables the pattern named. Matches join one per line in document order, which is kept rather than sorted: order that comes from the document is content. A pattern the grammar can only recover into an error node is refused rather than left to match nothing, and a pattern that matched no node at all is a hard error for the same reason an empty json selection is. Which languages a build can parse is a compile-time choice — see `lang`.

capture.description: Which of `ast`'s metavariables are the input, written without the `$` — `[NAME, ARGS]` for a pattern spelling `$NAME` and `$$$ARGS`. Absent means the whole matched node, which is the default; the list narrows each match to the parts it names, and is the only way to keep a construct's signature and drop a body the grammar glued to it. The pattern still decides which constructs match, so a metavariable left out of the list is still what makes the pattern reach them. Each capture renders as `($NAME …)` wrapping the rendering of every node bound to it, and the list is sorted before hashing — it is the set of parts that matter, so retyping it in another order is not an edit. A name the pattern does not define is a hard error naming what it does define: an undefined name binds nothing and would contribute the same bytes whatever the source said, and `allow_empty` cannot be blamed for it because the matches are all there. An anonymous `$$$` or a `$_` binds nothing in ast-grep and cannot be named at all.

lang.description: Which language `ast` parses the bytes as. Optional beside a `file` whose extension mmz recognises, required beside a `run` (a command line implies no language), and a manifest error without `ast`, which would be a key that silently does nothing. A grammar is not small — carrying every one would multiply the size of the binary — so each is a cargo feature and a stock build carries `rust` alone. Naming a language this build lacks is a hard error that names the feature flag to rebuild with; naming one mmz has no grammar for at all is a different error, because it needs a different answer. mmz never falls back to parsing an unknown file as something plausible.

allow_empty.description: Accept an input that measured nothing: with `json`, a selection that yielded no value or only null; with `ast`, a pattern that matched no node; with neither, stdout that is empty or only whitespace. One key, one meaning. By default it is an error, because it is the cheapest catch for a selector that matched nothing.

commands.description: Ordered command rules; the first token-prefix match wins.

name.description: Matcher and the cache identity. A single {scope} macro (one whitespace token, possibly embedded like --file={scope}) fans the rule over that scope's files: one per-file cache record per matched file, each keyed by the expanded name and scoped to that file plus the shared `inputs` pins.

inputs.description: Input names, each either a scope (whose globs union into this rule's file set) or a probe (whose stdout hash joins its digest) — one namespace, written identically. For a parametric rule these are the shared pins added to every per-file record; keep the fan scope out of them.

outputs.description: Literal artifact paths a successful run of this command is expected to produce, relative to the project root. The rule is fresh only when its inputs still hash the same AND every declared output exists, so an artifact deleted out from under a record (cargo clean, a fresh clone, a pruned target/) voids that record instead of leaving the rule fresh with nothing to show for it. Existence only — an output is never hashed. Each path is stat-ed, never walked, so the gitignore filter never applies to it and an artifact under an ignored tree needs no opt-out. Patterns are rejected at load: a glob here would never match. A run that exits 0 without producing a declared output is a hard error (exit 5) and records nothing.

match.description: How name matches argv. prefix (default): name's tokens are a leading slice of the command. exact: the whole command equals name's tokens.

tags.description: Free-form labels for filtering with `mmz --is-fresh --tag <tag>` (and `--status --tag <tag>`); repeat --tag to require every listed tag (AND). A rule with no tags never matches a --tag filter. Each tag is trimmed and blank entries are dropped; duplicates within one rule are rejected.

on_hit.description: Overrides the top-level on_hit for this rule. An empty string suppresses the cache-hit notice.
